sections.title: Functions of the lymphatic system
sections.highlight: Three functions: FLUID BALANCE (interstitial fluid returned to the blood as lymph), FAT ABSORPTION (lacteals carry chyle), DEFENSE (nodes filter lymph, the spleen filters blood).

sections.title: Components of the lymphatic system
sections.highlight: Six components: lymph, lymphatic vessels, lymph nodes, tonsils, spleen, thymus gland.

sections.title: Lymphatic capillaries & lymph formation
sections.highlight: Lymph moves ONE WAY: tissues → circulatory system. Lymphatic capillaries are closed-ended; their overlapping cells act as valves that let fluid in and stop backflow.

sections.title: Lymphatic vessels & how lymph moves
sections.highlight: Lymphatic vessels look like small veins and have one-way valves. COMPRESSION moves lymph: skeletal muscle, smooth muscle in the vessel wall, and thoracic pressure changes during breathing.

sections.title: Lymphatic ducts & drainage
sections.highlight: RIGHT LYMPHATIC DUCT: right upper limb + right head, neck, chest → right subclavian vein. THORACIC DUCT: everything else → left subclavian vein.

sections.title: Tonsils
sections.highlight: PALATINE: each side of the oral cavity. PHARYNGEAL (adenoid): near the internal opening of the nasal cavity. LINGUAL: posterior surface of the tongue. Together: a protective ring around the nasal and oral cavities.

sections.title: Lymph nodes: location
sections.highlight: Three superficial groups on each side: CERVICAL (neck), AXILLARY (armpit), INGUINAL (groin). Lymph passes through nodes before it enters the blood.

sections.title: Lymph node structure
sections.highlight: Capsule → trabeculae divide the node into compartments. Lymphatic TISSUE holds lymphocytes (nodules); lymphatic SINUSES hold macrophages. Several AFFERENT vessels in, ONE EFFERENT vessel out.

sections.title: Functions of lymph nodes
sections.highlight: Two functions: (1) ACTIVATION of the immune system: lymphocytes divide in germinal centers; (2) REMOVAL of pathogens by macrophages.

sections.title: The spleen: location & functions
sections.highlight: Size of a clenched fist, LEFT SUPERIOR corner of the abdomen. Filters blood, responds to foreign substances, destroys old RBCs, blood reservoir.

sections.title: Structure of the spleen: white pulp vs red pulp
sections.highlight: WHITE pulp = lymphatic tissue around ARTERIES (makes more lymphocytes). RED pulp = macrophages + RBCs, connects to VEINS (phagocytosis of foreign substances and worn-out RBCs).

sections.title: The thymus gland
sections.highlight: Bilobed, in the mediastinum behind the sternum. CORTEX (near capsule) = many lymphocytes; MEDULLA (center) = fewer. T lymphocytes, hormone THYMOSIN; T-cell production declines later in life.

sections.title: Overview: 8 processes of the lymphatic system
sections.highlight: 1 lymph forms · 2 nodes filter lymph · 3 lacteals absorb lipids (chyle) · 4 thoracic duct → blood · 5 spleen filters blood · 6 B cells and pre-T cells from red bone marrow · 7 pre-T cells mature in the thymus · 8 B and T cells populate lymphatic tissues.

recall.q: Name the three functions of the lymphatic system.
recall.a: Fluid balance, fat absorption, and defense.

recall.q: What is lymph, according to the fluid-balance function?
recall.a: Interstitial fluid that did not return to the blood capillaries, picked up by the lymphatic system and returned to the blood.

recall.q: What are lacteals and what is the fluid in them called?
recall.a: Lymphatic vessels that absorb lipids from the digestive tract; the fluid is chyle.

recall.q: Which structure filters lymph and which filters blood?
recall.a: Lymph nodes filter lymph; the spleen filters blood.

recall.q: List the six components of the lymphatic system.
recall.a: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, lymph nodes, tonsils, spleen, thymus gland.

recall.q: How does the slide define lymph?
recall.a: Fluid that enters lymphatic capillaries, composed of water and some solutes.

recall.q: Which lymph node groups are labelled on the whole-body figure?
recall.a: Cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes.

recall.q: In which direction does the lymphatic system carry fluid?
recall.a: One direction only: from the tissues to the circulatory system.

recall.q: Describe a lymphatic capillary.
recall.a: Tiny, closed-ended vessel in most tissues; overlapping squamous cells act as valves letting fluid in and preventing backflow; capillaries join to form lymphatic vessels.

recall.q: Where does the fluid that enters lymphatic capillaries come from?
recall.a: It moved out of blood capillaries into the tissue spaces.

recall.q: What do lymphatic capillaries join to form?
recall.a: Lymphatic vessels.

recall.q: Which blood vessels do lymphatic vessels resemble?
recall.a: Small veins.

recall.q: Name the three causes of compression that move lymph forward.
recall.a: Contraction of surrounding skeletal muscles; contraction of smooth muscle in the lymphatic vessels; pressure changes in the thorax during breathing.

recall.q: What keeps lymph moving in one direction inside lymphatic vessels?
recall.a: One-way valves.

recall.q: Which body regions drain into the right lymphatic duct?
recall.a: The right upper limb and the right side of the head, neck, and chest.

recall.q: Where does the right lymphatic duct empty?
recall.a: Into the right subclavian vein.

recall.q: What does the thoracic duct collect, and where does it empty?
recall.a: Lymph from all remaining lymphatic vessels that do not enter the right lymphatic duct; it empties into the left subclavian vein.

recall.q: Name the three tonsils.
recall.a: Palatine, pharyngeal, and lingual.

recall.q: Where is each tonsil located?
recall.a: Palatine: each side of the oral cavity. Pharyngeal: near the internal opening of the nasal cavity. Lingual: posterior surface of the tongue.

recall.q: Which tonsil is the adenoid?
recall.a: The pharyngeal tonsil.

recall.q: What do the tonsils form together?
recall.a: A protective ring of lymphatic tissue around the nasal and oral cavities.

recall.q: Name the three superficial aggregations of lymph nodes and where each is.
recall.a: Cervical (neck), axillary (axilla/armpit), inguinal (groin).

recall.q: Where are lymph nodes located in relation to lymphatic vessels?
recall.a: Along the lymphatic vessels.

recall.q: What must lymph pass through before entering the blood?
recall.a: Lymph nodes.

recall.q: What surrounds a lymph node, and what divides it into compartments?
recall.a: A dense connective tissue capsule; extensions of the capsule called trabeculae divide it.

recall.q: What is the difference between lymphatic tissue and lymphatic sinuses in a node?
recall.a: Lymphatic tissue contains lymphocytes and other cells forming lymphatic nodules; lymphatic sinuses are spaces between the nodules containing macrophages.

recall.q: How does lymph enter and leave a lymph node?
recall.a: It enters through several afferent vessels and exits through one efferent vessel.

recall.q: What are the two functions of lymph nodes?
recall.a: Activation of the immune system, and removal of pathogens through the action of macrophages.

recall.q: Where in a lymph node do lymphocytes divide?
recall.a: In the germinal centers of the nodules.

recall.q: Where do newly produced lymphocytes go?
recall.a: They are released into lymph, enter the blood stream, and then enter other lymphatic tissue.

recall.q: Where is the spleen and how big is it?
recall.a: In the left, superior corner of the abdomen; about the size of a clenched fist.

recall.q: List the four functions of the spleen on the slide.
recall.a: Filters blood; detects and responds to foreign substances; destroys old red blood cells; serves as a blood reservoir.

recall.q: Which lymphatic organ filters blood rather than lymph?
recall.a: The spleen.

recall.q: What are the two tissue types in the spleen?
recall.a: White pulp and red pulp.

recall.q: Describe white pulp.
recall.a: Lymphatic tissue surrounding arteries that can be stimulated to produce more lymphocytes.

recall.q: Describe red pulp.
recall.a: Contains macrophages and red blood cells, connects to veins; filters out foreign substances and worn-out red blood cells and destroys them by phagocytosis.

recall.q: Where is the thymus gland located?
recall.a: In the mediastinum, behind the sternum.

recall.q: How do the cortex and medulla of the thymus differ?
recall.a: Cortex: near the capsule, numerous lymphocytes. Medulla: toward the center, fewer lymphocytes.

recall.q: Which hormone influences T lymphocytes in the thymus?
recall.a: Thymosin.

recall.q: What happens to T-cell production later in life?
recall.a: It declines.

recall.q: Why is the lymph in lacteals called chyle?
recall.a: Because of its high lipid content.

recall.q: Where are B cells produced and where do they mature?
recall.a: Both in the red bone marrow.

recall.q: Where are pre-T cells produced, and where do they mature?
recall.a: Produced in the bone marrow; they migrate to the thymus and mature there into T cells.

recall.q: What do lymph nodes remove from lymph, and in which direction is the lymph flowing?
recall.a: Pathogens and debris, as the lymph flows toward the thoracic cavity.

recall.q: What happens to B cells and T cells after they mature?
recall.a: They circulate to, and populate, other lymphatic tissues.

Fluid that enters lymphatic capillaries, composed of water and some solutes
Lipid-rich fluid found only in the spleen
quiz.explanation: L5: lymph is 'fluid that enters lymphatic capillaries composed of water and some solutes'.

quiz.stem: Which set contains only components of the lymphatic system?
options: Lymph nodes, tonsils, spleen, thymus gland
Thymus gland, thyroid gland, spleen, lymph
Lymph nodes, tonsils, liver, thymus gland
quiz.explanation: L5 lists lymph, lymphatic vessels, lymph nodes, tonsils, spleen, and thymus gland.

quiz.stem: On the whole-body figure of the lymphatic system, the lymphatic vessels labelled in the intestinal wall are the:
quiz.explanation: Fig 14.1a (L4) labels 'Lacteals in intestinal wall'.

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly describes the direction of lymph flow?
options: Back and forth between the tissues and the lymph nodes
One direction, from the circulatory system to the tissues
In a closed circuit, like blood
One direction, from the tissues to the circulatory system
quiz.explanation: L6: lymphatic vessels carry fluid 'in one direction from tissues to circulatory system'.

quiz.stem: What feature of lymphatic capillaries lets fluid enter easily but prevents it from leaking back out?
options: Overlapping squamous cells that act as valves
A thick layer of smooth muscle
quiz.explanation: L6: 'overlapping squamous cells acts as valves to allow fluid in and prevent backflow'.

quiz.stem: Lymphatic capillaries are best described as:
options: Vessels that carry fluid toward the tissues
Large vessels open at both ends
Vessels found only in the digestive tract
quiz.explanation: L6: lymphatic capillaries are 'tiny, closed-ended vessels' found in most tissues.

quiz.stem: Which sequence best describes how lymph is formed and moved?
options: Blood capillaries → tissue spaces → lymphatic capillaries → lymphatic vessels
Lymphatic capillaries → blood capillaries → tissue spaces → lymphatic vessels
Lymphatic vessels → lymphatic capillaries → tissue spaces → blood capillaries
Tissue spaces → blood capillaries → lymphatic vessels → lymphatic capillaries
quiz.explanation: L6: fluid moves from blood capillaries into tissue spaces, enters lymphatic capillaries, and these join to form lymphatic vessels.

quiz.stem: All of the following describe lymphatic capillaries, EXCEPT:
options: They are absent from most tissues
They join to form lymphatic vessels
quiz.explanation: L6: lymphatic capillaries are 'in most tissues'.

quiz.stem: Lymphatic vessels most closely resemble:
quiz.explanation: L8: lymphatic vessels 'resemble small veins'.

quiz.stem: All of the following cause the compression that moves lymph forward, EXCEPT:
options: Pressure changes in the thorax during breathing
Contraction of smooth muscle in lymphatic vessels
Pumping action of the heart on lymphatic vessels
quiz.explanation: L8 lists three causes: skeletal muscle contraction, smooth muscle in the lymphatic vessels, and thoracic pressure changes during breathing.

quiz.stem: A patient is on strict bed rest and barely moves the lower limbs. Which mechanism of lymph movement in the legs is most directly reduced?
options: Pressure changes in the thorax during breathing
Overlapping squamous cells of the capillaries
Filtering of lymph by lymph nodes
quiz.explanation: L8: contraction of surrounding skeletal muscles compresses lymphatic vessels and moves lymph forward.

quiz.stem: Which combination of features belongs to lymphatic vessels?
options: Surrounded by a capsule; divided by trabeculae
Closed-ended; made of overlapping squamous cells only
Resemble small arteries; have no valves
Resemble small veins; have one-way valves
quiz.explanation: L8: lymphatic vessels resemble small veins and have one-way valves.

quiz.stem: During deep breathing, lymph movement is helped by:
quiz.explanation: L8: 'Pressure changes in the thorax during breathing' compress lymphatic vessels.

quiz.stem: Lymph from the right upper limb returns to the blood through the:
options: Thoracic duct, into the left subclavian vein
Right lymphatic duct, into the right subclavian vein
Thoracic duct, into the right subclavian vein
Right lymphatic duct, into the left subclavian vein
quiz.explanation: L9: vessels from the right upper limb empty into the right lymphatic duct, which empties into the right subclavian vein.

quiz.stem: A patient has an infected wound on the left foot. Lymph from that foot returns to the blood through which duct and vein?
options: Right lymphatic duct; right subclavian vein
Right lymphatic duct; left subclavian vein
quiz.explanation: L9: the thoracic duct collects lymph from all vessels that do not enter the right lymphatic duct (which drains only the right upper limb and right head, neck, chest) and empties into the left subclavian vein. Fig 14.1b (L10) shows the lower limbs in the thoracic-duct area.

quiz.stem: A patient has an infected cut on the RIGHT foot. Which duct receives lymph from that foot?
options: Neither duct; it enters the spleen
quiz.explanation: L9: the right lymphatic duct drains only the right upper limb and right head, neck, and chest. Everything else, including the right lower limb (Fig 14.1b, L10), goes to the thoracic duct.

quiz.stem: The thoracic duct empties into the:
quiz.explanation: L9: the thoracic duct 'empties into left subclavian vein'.

quiz.stem: All of the following drain into the right lymphatic duct, EXCEPT the:
options: Right side of the head and neck
quiz.explanation: L9: the right lymphatic duct receives the right upper limb and right head, neck, chest. The remaining vessels drain to the thoracic duct.

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the two lymphatic ducts?
options: Both ducts empty into the left subclavian vein
The thoracic duct drains only the thorax; the right lymphatic duct drains the rest
The right lymphatic duct drains the whole right half of the body; the thoracic duct drains the left half
The right lymphatic duct drains the right upper limb and right head, neck, and chest; the thoracic duct drains the rest
quiz.explanation: L9 and Fig 14.1b (L10): only the right upper quadrant goes to the right lymphatic duct.

quiz.stem: A tumor compresses the thoracic duct near where it ends. Based on the slides, lymph from which of these regions would still reach the blood normally?
quiz.explanation: L9: the right upper limb drains through the right lymphatic duct into the right subclavian vein, not through the thoracic duct.

quiz.stem: Which tonsil is located near the internal opening of the nasal cavity?
quiz.explanation: L11: 'pharyngeal tonsil near internal opening of nasal cavity (adenoid)'.

quiz.stem: The term 'adenoid' refers to the:
quiz.explanation: L11: the pharyngeal tonsil is labelled '(adenoid)'.

quiz.stem: Which pair correctly matches a tonsil with its location?
options: Lingual tonsil: posterior surface of the tongue
Palatine tonsil: posterior surface of the tongue
Pharyngeal tonsil: each side of the oral cavity
Lingual tonsil: internal opening of the nasal cavity
quiz.explanation: L11: palatine = each side of oral cavity; pharyngeal = near internal opening of nasal cavity; lingual = posterior surface of tongue.

quiz.stem: A clinician looks into a patient's open mouth and sees a mass of lymphatic tissue on each side of the oral cavity. These are the:
quiz.explanation: L11: palatine tonsils are 'on each side of oral cavity'.

quiz.stem: Together, the tonsils form a protective ring of lymphatic tissue around the:
quiz.explanation: L11: the tonsils 'form a protective ring of lymphatic tissue around nasal and oral cavities'.

quiz.stem: A patient notices rounded lumps in the armpit. Which superficial group of lymph nodes is located there?
quiz.explanation: L13: 'Axillary nodes in the axilla (armpit)'.

quiz.stem: Which pair correctly matches a lymph node group with its location?
quiz.explanation: L13: cervical = neck, axillary = armpit, inguinal = groin.

quiz.stem: Lymph passes through which structures before entering the blood?
quiz.explanation: L13: 'lymph passes through lymph nodes before entering blood'.

quiz.stem: All of the following are superficial aggregations of lymph nodes named on the slides, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: L13 names cervical, axillary, and inguinal nodes. 'Lingual' is a tonsil (L11).

quiz.stem: Lymph enters a lymph node through ______ and leaves through ______.
options: several afferent vessels; one efferent vessel
one afferent vessel; several efferent vessels
one afferent vessel; one efferent vessel
several efferent vessels; one afferent vessel
quiz.explanation: L14: 'Lymph enters a lymph node through several afferent vessels and exits through one efferent' vessel.

quiz.stem: The extensions of the capsule that divide a lymph node into compartments are called:
quiz.explanation: L14: 'Extensions of the capsule called trabeculae, divide the node into compartments.'

quiz.stem: In a lymph node, macrophages are contained in the:
quiz.explanation: L14: lymphatic sinuses are 'spaces between the nodules that contain macrophages'.

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes lymphatic tissue from lymphatic sinuses in a lymph node?
options: Lymphatic tissue forms the capsule; sinuses form the trabeculae
Lymphatic tissue carries lymph into the node; sinuses carry it out
Lymphatic tissue contains macrophages only; sinuses contain lymphocytes that form nodules
Lymphatic tissue contains lymphocytes that form nodules; sinuses are spaces between nodules that contain macrophages
quiz.explanation: L14 gives both definitions.

quiz.stem: Which sequence best describes the path of lymph through a lymph node?
options: Afferent vessels → efferent vessel → lymph node
Lymph node → afferent vessels → efferent vessel
Efferent vessel → lymph node → afferent vessels
Afferent vessels → lymph node → efferent vessel
quiz.explanation: L14: lymph enters through several afferent vessels and exits through one efferent vessel.

quiz.stem: A lymph node is surrounded by a:
quiz.explanation: L14: each node 'is surrounded by a dense connective tissue capsule'.

quiz.stem: During an infection, pathogens filtered out by a lymph node stimulate lymphocytes to divide. Where in the node does this division occur?
quiz.explanation: L15: filtered pathogens 'can stimulate lymphocytes to divide in the germinal centers of the nodules'.

quiz.stem: Which sequence best describes the route of newly produced lymphocytes from a lymph node?
options: Lymph → blood stream → other lymphatic tissue
Blood stream → red bone marrow → lymph
quiz.explanation: L15: 'Newly produced lymphocytes are released into lymph, enter the blood stream, and then enter other lymphatic tissue.'

quiz.stem: In lymph nodes, removal of pathogens is carried out through the action of:
quiz.explanation: L15: 'Removal of pathogens through the action of macrophages'.

quiz.stem: Which pair lists the two functions of lymph nodes given on the slides?
options: Absorption of lipids; storage of blood
Production of chyle; secretion of thymosin
Maturation of T cells; destruction of old red blood cells
Activation of the immune system; removal of pathogens by macrophages
quiz.explanation: L15 lists these two functions.

quiz.stem: The spleen is located in the:
options: Right, superior corner of the abdomen
Left, superior corner of the abdomen
Left, inferior corner of the abdomen
quiz.explanation: L17: the spleen is 'located in the left, superior corner of the abdomen'.

quiz.stem: All of the following are functions of the spleen listed on the slides, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: L17 lists filtering blood, detecting and responding to foreign substances, destroying old RBCs, and blood reservoir. T-cell maturation is in the thymus (L20, L22).

quiz.stem: Which lymphatic organ destroys old red blood cells and serves as a blood reservoir?
quiz.explanation: L17 lists both as functions of the spleen.

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the spleen from a lymph node?
options: The spleen filters blood; lymph nodes filter lymph
The spleen filters lymph; lymph nodes filter blood
quiz.explanation: L17: the spleen filters blood. L3 and L22: lymph nodes filter lymph.

quiz.stem: The size of the spleen is compared on the slides to a:
quiz.explanation: L17: 'size of clenched fist'.

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes white pulp from red pulp?
options: White pulp is lymphatic tissue surrounding arteries; red pulp contains macrophages and red blood cells and connects to veins
White pulp contains macrophages and red blood cells; red pulp is lymphatic tissue surrounding arteries
White pulp connects to veins; red pulp surrounds the capsule
White pulp destroys worn-out red blood cells; red pulp produces lymphocytes
quiz.explanation: L18 gives both definitions.

quiz.stem: Worn-out red blood cells are filtered out and destroyed in which part of the spleen?
quiz.explanation: L18: red pulp 'filters out foreign substances and worn-out red blood cells and destroys them by phagocytosis'.

quiz.stem: Which part of the spleen can be stimulated to produce more lymphocytes?
quiz.explanation: L18: white pulp is 'lymphatic tissue surrounding arteries that can be stimulated to produce more lymphocytes'.

quiz.stem: By what process does the red pulp destroy foreign substances and worn-out red blood cells?
quiz.explanation: L18: red pulp 'destroys them by phagocytosis'.

quiz.stem: A blood sample shows that old red blood cells are being removed normally. Which splenic tissue, and which of its cells, does the slide credit for this?
quiz.explanation: L18: red pulp contains macrophages and red blood cells and destroys worn-out red blood cells by phagocytosis.

quiz.stem: White pulp surrounds ______, while red pulp connects to ______.
quiz.explanation: L18: white pulp is lymphatic tissue surrounding arteries; red pulp connects to veins.

quiz.stem: The thymus gland is located in the:
options: Left superior corner of the abdomen
quiz.explanation: L20: 'bilobed gland located in mediastinum behind the sternum'.

quiz.stem: Which hormone influences T lymphocytes in the thymus?
quiz.explanation: L20: T lymphocytes are acted on 'under the influence of the hormone thymosin'.

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the cortex from the medulla of the thymus?
options: The cortex contains macrophages only; the medulla contains red blood cells
The cortex is toward the center and has fewer lymphocytes; the medulla is near the capsule and has numerous
The cortex contains red pulp; the medulla contains white pulp
The cortex is near the capsule and has numerous lymphocytes; the medulla is toward the center and has fewer
quiz.explanation: L20 gives both descriptions.

quiz.stem: An 80-year-old is compared with a 10-year-old. Based on the slides, which statement about the thymus is expected?
options: Production of T cells is lower in the 80-year-old
The thymus of the 80-year-old has moved into the abdomen
Thymosin now acts on red blood cells
Production of T cells is higher in the 80-year-old
quiz.explanation: L20: 'Production of T cells declines later in life.'

quiz.stem: In the thymus, trabeculae divide each lobe into:
quiz.explanation: L20: each lobe 'has trabeculae that divides each lobe into lobules'.

quiz.stem: Which lymphatic organ is described as bilobed?
quiz.explanation: L20: the thymus is a 'bilobed gland'.

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes B cells from pre-T cells, according to the summary slide?
options: B cells are produced and mature in the red bone marrow; pre-T cells are produced in the bone marrow and mature in the thymus
Both are produced in the spleen and mature in the lymph nodes
B cells mature in the thymus; pre-T cells mature in the spleen
B cells are produced in the thymus; pre-T cells are produced and mature in the red bone marrow
quiz.explanation: L22 steps 6 and 7.

quiz.stem: Lymph in the lacteals is referred to as chyle because of its:
quiz.explanation: L22 step 3: 'referred to as chyle due to the high lipid content'.

quiz.stem: Which sequence best describes the development of a T cell on the summary slide?
options: Pre-T cell produced in spleen → enters blood → migrates to lymph node → matures into T cell
Pre-T cell produced in bone marrow → matures in bone marrow → migrates to thymus
Pre-T cell produced in bone marrow → enters blood → migrates to thymus → matures into T cell
Pre-T cell produced in thymus → enters lymph → migrates to bone marrow → matures into T cell
quiz.explanation: L22 steps 6 and 7: pre-T cells are produced in the bone marrow, enter the blood, and migrate to the thymus where they mature.

quiz.stem: Lymph nodes filter lymph as it flows toward the:
quiz.explanation: L22 step 2: lymph nodes filter lymph 'as the lymph flows toward the thoracic cavity'.

quiz.stem: At which site do lacteals absorb lipids?
quiz.explanation: L22 step 3: lacteals 'absorb lipids at the small intestine'.

quiz.stem: Which organ is described as a site where lymphocytes respond to infections and where blood is filtered?
quiz.explanation: L22 step 5: 'The spleen filters blood and is a site where lymphocytes respond to infections.'

quiz.stem: A child is born without a functioning thymus. Based on the summary slide, which step fails most directly?
options: Pre-T cells maturing into T cells
B cells maturing in the red bone marrow
quiz.explanation: L22 step 7: 'Pre-T cells migrate to the thymus where they mature to become T cells.'

quiz.stem: Which sequence best describes how chyle reaches the blood?
options: Lacteals → larger lymphatic vessels such as the thoracic duct → blood
Blood capillaries → lacteals → lymph nodes → tissues
quiz.explanation: L22 steps 3 and 4: lacteals absorb lipids; lymph, including chyle, passes into larger vessels such as the thoracic duct and then enters the blood.

quiz.stem: All of the following are true of the processes on the summary slide, EXCEPT:
options: B cells mature in the red bone marrow
T cells mature in the red bone marrow
quiz.explanation: L22 step 7: pre-T cells mature in the thymus, not in the bone marrow.

Empties into the left subclavian vein
Receives lymph from the right side of the head and neck
Collects lymph from the remaining vessels that do not enter the other duct
Empties into the right subclavian vein
Its area in Fig 14.1b includes both lower limbs

Near the internal opening of the nasal cavity
Posterior surface of the tongue
Also called the adenoid
Filter lymph, removing pathogens and debris
Filters blood

quiz.title: Tissue regions of the lymphatic organs

items.prompt: Lymphatic tissue surrounding arteries
Contains macrophages and red blood cells; connects to veins
Near the capsule; numerous lymphocytes
Toward the center; fewer lymphocytes
Spaces between nodules that contain macrophages
Where stimulated lymphocytes divide in a lymph node

flags.text: L20 says the thymus "produces and matures T lymphocytes". L22 (steps 6-7) says pre-T cells are produced in the bone marrow and only mature in the thymus. No question here depends on where T cells are "produced"; the site uses L22 for the sequence.
L9 names the "right lymphatic duct". Fig 14.7 on L23 labels "Thoracic duct or right lymphatic trunks". The site uses L9's wording.
L6 says "overlapping squamous cells" act as valves; Fig 14.2b (L7) labels the same thing "overlapping epithelial cells". Same structure, two wordings.
The "cortex" of the lymph node appears only as a label in Fig 14.4. L14's text never uses the word, and no slide in L3-L23 names a lymph node medulla.
Fig 14.1a labels the "mammary plexus" and "bone marrow", but no slide in L3-L23 explains the mammary plexus.
Lymph is defined only as "water and some solutes". Its detailed composition is not given beyond the solutes listed on L3.
The slides do not say how many of each tonsil there are (only "on each side" for the palatine tonsils), and tonsillitis or tonsil removal is not on any slide.
Removal or rupture of the spleen is not on any slide. Edema as a named condition is not on any slide in L3-L23 either; scenario questions only ask which slide-listed function or pathway is involved.
"collects lymph from the from remaining lymphatic vessels" read as "from the remaining".
"Each nodes is surrounded" and "one efferent vessels" read as "Each node" and "one efferent vessel".
